title: Ziina Launches Split Bill to Simplify Shared Group Payments
snippet: UAE fintech Ziina launches Split Bill, letting users divide group expenses, automate payment reminders, and track settlements as annual volume tops $2 billion. The post Ziina Launches Split Bill to Simplify Shared Group Payments appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Homegrown UAE financial platform Ziina has launched Split Bill, a new feature extending its consumer peer-to-peer (P2P) offering to streamline how users request, track, and settle shared group expenses. The rollout comes as the Dubai-headquartered fintech crosses major operational milestones, reaching over one million annual users and surpassing US$2 billion in annualized payment volume.

Managing group expenses frequently leaves a single organizer responsible for calculating shares, tracking incoming transfers, and chasing late payers. According to Ziina’s internal user research, asking friends to settle up represents the biggest friction point in shared spending—with some respondents noting they would rather absorb an expense than repeatedly remind peers to pay. Furthermore, 71 per cent of surveyed consumers reported splitting expenses at least once a month, while all interviewed participants indicated they rely on WhatsApp to coordinate shared bills across disconnected channels.

Automating Reminders and Cross-Platform Settlements

Split Bill centralizes expense division, payment requests, and automated follow-ups within a single interface. Available for purchases made using a Ziina Card as well as external payment methods, the feature allows organizers to allocate specific shares to each participant and monitor real-time settlement progress.

Key operational capabilities of the feature include:

In-App and Guest Checkout: Existing Ziina account holders can settle their share directly inside the mobile app, while non-users can pay via a dedicated web link using a debit card, Apple Pay, or Google Pay.

Automated Follow-Ups: The platform automatically dispatches payment reminders to outstanding participants, removing the social friction of manual follow-ups from the organizer.

Real-Time Tracking: Organizers can view individual contribution statuses as funds arrive and receive instant notifications once the entire group bill has been settled.

“We build products around real customer behaviour, identifying opportunities to make familiar financial interactions simpler and more intuitive,” stated Faisal Toukan, CEO and co-founder of Ziina. “Our user research showed us that asking friends to pay can be the hardest part of splitting an expense. With Split Bill, we’re addressing that everyday friction by making it easier for people to organise shared expenses, track contributions and settle up.”

Surging P2P Velocity and Smaller-Value Group Transfers

The launch capitalizes on rapid growth in everyday P2P activity across Ziina’s user base. During the first ten months of 2026, total P2P transfers on the platform climbed 330 per cent year-on-year, while the number of active senders and recipients grew by 220 per cent. Monthly P2P transfer volumes also recorded seven consecutive months of growth between April and October 2026.

Underlying transaction metrics point directly toward higher-frequency, everyday group spending:

Shift to Micro-Transfers: Ziina’s median P2P payment value declined by 33 per cent year-on-year, while the share of transfers valued at AED 200 or less increased by 16 per cent.

Spike in Multi-Party Settlements: Between August and October 2026, instances of users receiving payments from two or more friends on the same day surged 500 per cent year-on-year, accounting for 10 per cent of all P2P transfers executed on the platform.

UAE Digital P2P Momentum and Full-Stack Scale

Ziina’s product expansion aligns with a broader structural shift away from cash across the Emirates. Central Bank of the UAE (CBUAE) data recorded 114.9 million customer-to-customer transfers in 2025, up from 109.7 million in 2024. Meanwhile, Visa’s 2026 Where Cash Hides study revealed that digital adoption within the P2P category rose by five percentage points to reach 35 per cent.

Founded in 2020 by Faisal Toukan, Sarah Toukan, and Talal Toukan—and recently recognized with the 2026 Dubai-it Award presented by His Highness Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Crown Prince of Dubai—Ziina operates under CBUAE regulatory authorizations spanning Stored Value Facilities, Retail Payment Services Category III, and Exchange Business Category IV. By pairing licensed payment infrastructure with social, behavior-led features like Split Bill, the company continues to consolidate everyday consumer spending and merchant acquiring into a unified financial ecosystem.

FCA to explore quantum computing to tackle financial crime

              

  

  

  
    

        

    

      

A new initiative will bring together firms, quantum technology providers, and national research labs to explore practical applications of quantum computing.

  

            						

The FCA will bring together financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories to explore how quantum computing could help tackle financial crime.

The Quantum Experimentation Group, the first of its kind for a regulator, will initially explore how quantum machine learning could help detect money laundering and fraud. It will launch in the first quarter of 2027.

Participants will use an FCA synthetic dataset – artificially generated data – to help overcome a key barrier to testing: access to suitable data.

The group will help firms explore practical uses of quantum computing in financial services and share findings to guide future testing. It will also help the FCA understand the technology’s opportunities and limitations, barriers to experimentation and what these could mean for regulation.

Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'We want to help firms explore where quantum could make a meaningful difference, and early experimentation is essential to understanding its potential in financial services. By bringing together firms, technology providers and researchers we can build readiness and identify practical applications for common industry challenges, starting with financial crime.'

The initiative builds on the FCA’s research into the long-term potential of quantum computing in financial services.

Financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories can register their interest in joining the group by 31 December 2026.

Notes to editors

Read more about the Quantum Experimentation Group and how to register an interest in joining the group.

The FCA’s Quantum Experimentation Group will be the world’s first regulator-led quantum computing experimentation group.

The group will support organisations at different stages of their quantum journey, from those beginning to explore potential use cases to those already undertaking advanced experimentation.

As part of the initiative, the FCA will define problem statements and work alongside participants to build understanding of the opportunities, limitations and practical considerations associated with quantum technologies.

The initiative will complement wider activity across the UK’s quantum ecosystem by creating additional opportunities for collaborative experimentation and learning.

title: From wallet to full-stack fintech: Murtaza Ali on JazzCash’s path to 2030
snippet: Murtaza Ali, CEO of JazzCash, on 64 million users, lending, insurance and government payments in Pakistan, and the road to 2030. The Fintech Times SFF 2026 cover story. The post From wallet to full-stack fintech: Murtaza Ali on JazzCash’s path to 2030 appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Mobile money has shown it can reach people with no bank account. The harder test in emerging markets is whether it can then give them credit, insurance and savings, and carry government payments too. 

In Pakistan, JazzCash has become one of the clearest answers, growing from a basic mobile wallet into a platform that handles payments, lending, insurance, merchant services and government disbursements at national scale.

Operating as a standalone entity and partnering with Mobilink Microfinance Bank, JazzCash is a core pillar of VEON’s digital operator strategy. It was recently named among the World’s Top Fintech Companies 2026 by CNBC and Statista in the Payments category.

In this exclusive interview, Murtaza Ali, CEO of JazzCash, discusses the platform’s evolution, the shift to a cashless economy, the role of lending, insurance and social protection in financial inclusion, and the road to becoming a full-stack fintech by 2030.

This interview is the cover story of The Fintech Times Singapore Fintech Festival 2026 Special Edition, distributed at Singapore EXPO from 18 to 20 November 2026. Read the full edition here. 

JazzCash began in 2012 as a basic mobile wallet. How would you describe the journey to where the platform stands today?

It has been a steady expansion of what customers needed from us. In the early years the focus was on fundamentals: money transfers, and bill payments. Once that foundation was trusted, we moved into merchant acquiring, digital payments, consumer lending, remittances and a debit card. From there we added a payment gateway, insurance, merchant lending, buy now pay later and cross-border payments.

Today JazzCash serves 64 million users, and one in three adults in Pakistan uses it. None of this was built in isolation. We built each product around a task people already did in cash or in queues, and made it work from a phone.

We did not set out to build a long list of products. We set out to solve the next real problem for the customer.

JazzCash processes the equivalent of 16% of Pakistan’s GDP and one in every three e-commerce payments. What explains this level of adoption?

Trust and convenience, built on a distribution network that is hard to replicate. Our agent and merchant footprint puts JazzCash within reach of people who have never had a bank branch nearby. On top of that, we process more than 16 million transactions a day, up 68% year on year, so reliability has to be constant.

E-commerce is a good example. JazzCash has 2,000+ online merchants including food delivery, ticketing and marketplaces. As volumes grow, so does our responsibility to know who is using the platform. Every merchant and aggregator goes through KYC and due diligence under State Bank of Pakistan rules, and transactions are monitored continuously. Customers don’t choose a payment method for the technology behind it. They choose the one that works every time.

More volume means more responsibility. Every merchant is verified and monitored.

Pakistan is pushing towards a cashless economy. What role does the merchant network play?

It is fundamental, because a wallet is only useful if there are places to spend from it. Pakistan has fewer than 200,000 card terminals for over 250 million people, and a card terminal rarely makes sense for a small roadside (kiryana) store or a home-based business. A printed or digital QR code does, with no hardware at all.

We now have 1.9 million merchants and over 8 million active QR users. We hold a significant volume of RAAST person-to-merchant QR payments, and monthly throughput has grown seven times. More than half of our merchants are onboarded through digital channels, and for those who need guidance, field teams help them get started under the same compliance standards. This work sits within the Prime Minister’s Cashless Economy Initiative, and our Chairman, Aamir Ibrahim, serves on the Prime Minister’s Task Force on Cashless Economy.

When a shopkeeper goes digital, the whole neighbourhood economy moves with them.

Digital lending is often seen as risky in emerging markets. How is JazzCash approaching it?

Carefully, and at scale. We issue more than 280,000 loans every day on an average, and our ReadyCash product won Silver for Banking at Money20/20 USA 2025. Over four million customers use the lending product each month, and 30% of borrowers are women.

These are small, short-term loans that help a household cover an emergency or a small business buy stock. Payments and wallet data help us lend to people the traditional system could not assess. The aim is to build credit history for people who had none, so responsible borrowing leads to better access over time.

Credit works best when it is small, fast, and built on a customer’s own financial behaviour.

Insurance penetration in Pakistan is below 1% of GDP, yet JazzCash sold over 1.3 million policies in a single day. What does that tell us?

That the demand for protection was always there. What was missing was a product that was simple, affordable and available where people already transact. Health insurance in Pakistan has traditionally been tied to formal employment, yet around 75% of the workforce is informal, and most private health spending, about 89%, is paid out of pocket. For a household with no savings buffer, one bad diagnosis can undo years of progress.

So we embedded insurance into the app and into everyday transactions, with products starting from PKR 3 a day, around one US cent, and the Sehat+ health platform backed by nearly 400 panel hospitals. During the 2025 monsoon floods, more than 43,000 policyholders received an instant relief payment directly in their wallets, the first digital claim payout of its kind in Pakistan. Today we reach 17.9 million policyholders and are the number one digital insurance distribution platform in the country, recognised as a winner for InsurTech at The Money Awards 2026.

Financial inclusion is not complete until people are protected, not just banked.

JazzCash is also a major partner for channelling government stipends and welfare. How did that come about?

It started with disaster relief for displaced families in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in 2021, and grew through our selection as a disbursement partner for the Benazir Income Support Programme, Pakistan’s largest social safety net. BISP pays a stipend to a woman in 12 million low-income households, and for years collecting it meant travelling to a campsite, spending around 10% of the grant on the commute, proving identity in person.

We rebuilt that journey. Beneficiaries are verified with CNIC and biometric checks, receive a free Jazz SIM pre-linked to a wallet, and the money lands directly in their own account. Direct wallet transfers have already reached PKR 20 billion for 1.48 million women, with no agent, no queue and no wait. Across all our government and development sector partnerships we serve more than 3 million beneficiaries, channelling over PKR 100 billion this year alone.

Getting paid should not cost a day’s wages. Dignity is part of the design.

Financial inclusion and poverty alleviation are central to the VEON narrative. What impact are you seeing?

For many customers, JazzCash is the first formal financial service they use, and women hold 35% of our accounts. For many beneficiaries, a government stipend is their first step into the digital economy, and the wallet then becomes a place to save, pay, borrow and get insured.

Poverty alleviation is not one product. It is access to a safe place to save, a way to receive money, credit to start or grow something, and insurance to protect it. When those come through one platform on a phone a person already owns, the barriers fall quickly.

Access to financial services is a foundation for a better life.

What lessons from JazzCash apply to VEON’s other markets?

The core lesson is to start with the customer’s daily need and build around the distribution you already have. Across VEON, 59 million active customers now use our financial services in Pakistan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, and Bangladesh is set to join with regulatory progress there.

Each market is at a different stage, but the playbook travels well: payments first, then the ecosystem around it. The value comes from sharing what works across the Group, including our partnership with Mastercard to scale AI-enabled financial services across four markets.

The model is portable. The customer insight has to be local.

Looking ahead to 2030, what is the vision for JazzCash?

The JazzCash app will work like a personal financial adviser: you talk to it, and it helps you pay bills, make idle money work and borrow when you need to.

Ask “What is due today?” and you’ll see your bills in one place and pay them with one tap or a voice command. If PKR 50,000 has sat untouched since the start of the month, the app will ask whether you’d like to move it into savings or a mutual fund. If a bill falls due before your next income arrives and your balance won’t cover it, the app will offer a small loan, with the cost shown upfront.

This is hyper-personalisation: customers who have never had access to investment or credit products will have it on their own screen, at the moment it matters. For people using AI in a financial app for the first time, trust comes first, so security has to be strict and data has to stay sovereign. We will not scale these features faster than we can secure them.

Your money should not sit idle, and your app should be the first to notice.

About JazzCash

JazzCash began in 2012 as a mobile wallet and now serves 64 million users in Pakistan, with payments, lending, insurance, merchant services and government disbursements. It is part of VEON and partners with Mobilink Microfinance Bank. jazzcash.com.pk

fullText:
Three themes stand out: the growing use of AI, innovation crossing traditional sector boundaries, and financial inclusion.

As firms develop new products, services and business models, many engage with us through our Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Pathways to understand how regulation applies to their proposition or to test innovative ideas in a controlled environment.

Looking across applications lets us observe emerging trends. It helps us understand how technologies are evolving, and identify emerging regulatory questions.

In turn, this supports our wider work and helps us keep pace with developments across financial services.

Applications at a glance

37% involved AI (up from 31% in 2025), making it the most common technology theme.

92% of the firms engaging with our services were doing so for the first time, highlighting continued demand from new innovators.

64% of proposed solutions included a retail element, showing continued focus on consumer-facing innovation.

The growing use of AI

Firms are focusing increasingly on how to deploy, oversee and govern AI in their business models.

They’re looking at how to use AI to help consumers better understand and manage their finances, support businesses with payment processes, and provide customers with more personalised guidance and support.

Regulation and innovation are working in tandem to deploy new technologies safely and build consumer protection into new products from the outset.

Innovation is becoming more interconnected

Innovation does not always fit neatly into traditional sector categories. While payments and digital assets represented the largest sector-specific portion of recent applications, cross-sector propositions have also been common, representing around one-third of applications.

Many firms are combining technologies, data, payments and consumer-facing services in new ways. As a result, innovative technologies are increasingly crossing traditional sector boundaries and requiring firms to consider how existing governance, accountability, data use and regulatory frameworks apply.

A recent example is our stablecoins cohort in the Regulatory Sandbox. Stablecoin business models often cut across traditional sector boundaries, combining elements of payments, digital assets, and financial market activity. The cohort brought together firms intending to issue UK stablecoins to test how proposed requirements could operate in practice and provide evidence to support policy development.

Financial inclusion

Firms continue to focus on how to improve consumer access to and engagement with financial services. They’re not only exploring new technologies, but also considering how these tools can help address practical consumer challenges.

Applications this year have included propositions aimed at improving consumer understanding, accessibility, personalised support, and access to financial services for underserved groups.

A large proportion of proposed solutions included a retail element, indicating that most firms remain focused on end consumers.

What we’re learning about Sandbox participation over time

We are looking beyond current application trends to understand the longer-term experience of firms that have participated in the Regulatory Sandbox.

Our preliminary research suggests that, as of September 2026, around 71% of them are still active. We are continuing this analysis to better understand the ongoing commercial success of participating firms and whether their original propositions have continued to operate.

We have also been looking to understand at which point of their growth firms engage with the Regulatory Sandbox.

We’ve found that the service is particularly relevant at an early stage of a firm’s development, with around 70% of applications coming from firms that are 0 to 2 years old.

Demand is strongest when firms are still developing their business models, products and approaches to compliance, and seeking to understand how regulation applies as they refine and validate innovative propositions.

Looking ahead

Applications to our Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Pathways give us an early view of the technologies, business models and the regulatory questions that firms are exploring.

They also provide insight into developments beyond the UK.

We’re continuing to engage with international firms seeking to enter the UK market and sharing insights with overseas regulators and innovation initiatives. This helps us to understand global innovation trends.

The trends we have seen so far suggest that innovation is scaling up, becoming more sophisticated, and more focused on addressing real-world consumer needs.

We’ll continue to engage with firms as technology develops. One way we’re doing this is through thematic cohorts, which explore key areas in greater depth.

Following our Regulatory Sandbox stablecoins cohort, applications to a new climate scenarios cohort opened on 1 October 2026. The cohort invites firms and specialists to test innovative approaches to climate scenario analysis and risk assessment, supporting wider work on sustainable finance and climate-related risks.

Firms developing new ideas should consider how existing regulation applies to their proposition, how they can test and scale innovation successfully, and what safeguards will deliver good outcomes for consumers and markets.

Our innovation services help firms answer these questions. They also let us test policy approaches and gather evidence on how regulation works in practice. This helps inform smarter, more proportionate regulation.

We’re here to support innovators across financial services, helping ensure the UK remains one of the best places in the world to develop, test and scale innovative propositions.

To find out more about our innovation services and keep up to date with future opportunities, visit our Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Pathways pages.

title: Insights2040 day two: regulators mark their own quantum homework
snippet: global toolkit showing most financial regulators are at an early stage on quantum, a payments industry report saying nobody yet owns the problem, and four questions GFTN is carrying into the Singapore Fintech Festival. The post Insights2040 day two: regulators mark their own quantum homework appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The closed-door meetings ended with a global toolkit showing most financial regulators are at an early stage on quantum, a payments industry report saying nobody yet owns the problem, and four questions GFTN is carrying into the Singapore Fintech Festival.

The second and final day of GFTN’s Insights2040 Annual Meetings was framed by the organiser around trust, scale and operational resilience: institutions putting enterprise AI, tokenised assets and cross-border stablecoins to work while defending against AI-enabled fraud and quantum threats. Only one of the day’s sessions produced a published document, and it turned the lens on the regulators themselves.

Twenty-five regulators, graded by their own hand

The Global Financial Innovation Network published its Project Otto Toolkit after a launch session at the Sands Expo and Convention Centre. Led by the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority with the Alberta Securities Commission, the British Columbia Securities Commission and India’s IFSCA, it asked 25 member regulators to assess their own maturity on quantum, in two areas: quantum security, meaning the threat to today’s encryption, and quantum innovation, meaning what the technology could do for finance.

The method is simple to describe. Regulators were scored against 42 measures grouped by what they say, what they do and how they engage with firms, on four levels from ad hoc to adaptive. The results are anonymised and the report is careful about its limits: self-assessed, not statistically representative and not a ranking.

The picture is of an early-stage field. Most respondents sit in the lower and middle of the range. Most score higher on security than on innovation. The most mature activity is the easiest one: 84 per cent, or 21 of the 25, are beyond the lowest level on attending events. On security, 76 per cent are beyond the lowest level on horizon scanning and on building internal capability, but no security measure has a most common score in the top two levels. On innovation, the most common score for most measures is the lowest, and hands-on engagement with firms through sandboxes, testing and proofs of concept is the weakest area of all.

“Regulators are building maturity through action rather than articulation,” the report says. Of the innovation side, it is blunter: “Quantum innovation is exploratory, not experimental.”

Four examples of practice are named, among them the Dubai Financial Services Authority’s Emerging Technology Risk Regulatory College, alongside a Canadian securities regulators’ working group, IFSCA’s innovation sandbox and the FCA’s repeatable supervisory assessment of firms’ readiness for post-quantum cryptography. In his foreword, Colin Payne, head of innovation at the FCA and GFIN chair, writes: “Our challenge is not to predict the quantum future with certainty, but to ensure we are prepared to shape it responsibly.”

The industry mirror

The payments industry published its own version of the same finding on the same day. The Emerging Payments Association Asia released From Awareness to Action: What Quantum-Safe Readiness Requires Now, the work of its quantum-safe cryptography working group.

Its argument is that awareness of the risk has not turned into action because nobody inside most organisations owns it. In the association’s own workshops last year, only 20 per cent of participants said their senior stakeholders were very familiar with the threat. The report also points to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s first Quantum Preparedness Index, which it says scored the territory’s banking sector 2.3 out of 10 in July.

The remedy is a 90-day list: name an accountable executive, start discovery in a handful of high-value systems, ask critical vendors for their post-quantum plans and dates, assess readiness across the organisation, and write cryptographic agility into contracts as they come up for renewal. “Awareness is growing, but ownership is still unclear,” said Camilla Bullock, the association’s chief executive. Payments make the problem harder than most, because every party in a chain has to move. As IBM’s Ray Harishankar put it, organisations are “only as ready as the vendors and counterparties with which they exchange messages”.

Put the two documents side by side and the week’s pattern holds. The standards exist and the cryptography exists. What is missing is someone accountable for using them.

Four bottlenecks

In its message to delegates, GFTN summarised two days of roundtables as work on four bottlenecks: how digital assets and stablecoins hold up under stress, who is accountable when autonomous AI agents transact, how to build services on top of interoperable payment rails, and how to close gaps in fraud defence and quantum readiness. It said the discussions would be carried forward across its forums in 2027.

The published agenda shows how those questions were framed. Sessions on the final day asked how cross-border stablecoin recognition can work, how tokenisation moves beyond issuance, who is accountable in an economy of AI agents and whether convertibility can hold under stress at scale. None of them is a question about whether the technology functions.

The Singapore Fintech Festival opens on Wednesday at Singapore EXPO, with Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong giving the ministerial keynote. The questions from the closed rooms now move to the public stages.

title: Checkouts are built for speed. Fraudsters are thankful.
snippet: Faster checkouts may win customers. But as friction drops, are we making fraud easier too?
fullText:
The frictionless conundrum 

The pursuit of higher conversion rates has given fraudsters an ideal playground –– high speed checkouts. 

As physical barriers fade, card-not-present (CNP) fraud rates have surged to 7.5x higher than in-person fraud, with global CNP fraud forecasted to hit $62.9 billion by 2027 according to Visa net data. 

Striving for "zero friction" without real-time back-end verification creates a massive liability. Stripping away user checks may shave off seconds, but it sets the stage for an escalating race to one-click convenience.

The race to one-click everything 

Consumer demand for instant, frictionless purchasing has made manual card entry nearly obsolete, with guest checkout dropping from 44% of e-commerce transactions in 2019 to just 16% by 2025. However, rushing to meet consumer expectations by reducing verification steps can create costly blind spots 

How every second removed from checkout removes another verification point

Stripping friction to accelerate checkout often compromises critical security controls with e-commerce merchants losing 3% of total revenue to fraud annually. To combat these losses, merchants rely on static fraud rules, as manual review remains far too slow for instant purchasing. 

But these rigid controls reject 6% of valid orders out of suspicion — turning away (and frustrating) legitimate buyers. The impact of this can be severe, as 35% of consumers abandon merchants permanently after a single false decline.

Therefore, less checkout verification does not mean less friction; it simply shifts it downstream. The 2026 Global eCommerce Payments and Fraud Report found that over 60% of merchants report rising first-party misuse (AKA friendly fraud), with the average cost to manage and resolve a single dispute surpassing $80. While merchants can shave seconds off checkout, they may pay a far steeper price post-checkout in operational drain, lost inventory and heavy chargeback fees. 

The rise of account takeover and synthetic identity fraud

As front-end verification is reduced, bad actors can exploit these unguarded perimeters at scale. 

Automated botnets now drive widespread credential abuse, impacting 65% of merchants while card testing affects 39% of sellers. Stored merchant accounts have become prime targets for account takeover –– which is the unauthorized hijacking of a customer’s account using stolen credentials. 

Furthermore, millisecond evaluation windows across instant payment rails leave little time for manual intervention, which can accelerate global online scam volume.

Why “frictionless” doesn’t mean “trustless”

To counter this, merchants should shift from visible user hurdles to background data verification — removing the burden from customers and enabling seamless authentication behind the scenes.

By combining real-time cardholder verification and token management to validate account details automatically, security can be embedded across the transaction lifecycle. 

For checkouts that balance speed and security, look for authentication and tokenization tools like: 

Payment Account & Status Validation: Confirms account status, credentials and expiration dates are active before authorization.

Name & Identity Verification (ANI): Matches checkout names with issuer records to prevent synthetic identity fraud.

Address Verification (AVS): Cross-checks billing address data against cardholder records to catch discrepancies.

Card Verification Value (CVV2): Verifies the three-digit code to confirm physical card possession.

Age & Attribute Verifications: Verifies key customer attributes to ensure compliant, secure onboarding.

Unified  Token Vault: Consolidates customer data, card details, and network tokens (Visa, Mastercard, Amex, JCB) into one secure token.

Omnichannel & Alternative Payment Support: Extends tokenization to alternative payment methods like ACH and eChecks, reducing PCI scope and integration complexity.

By validating details and securing credentials in the background, you can flag compromised accounts, boost authorization rates, and deliver a frictionless checkout experience.

The shift to “intelligent friction”

Ultimately, securing modern checkout is not about slowing buyers down but applying security smartly, where it matters most. Rather than trying to eliminate all friction, merchants should focus on "intelligent friction" minimizes friction for genuine customers while adding more checks for higher-risk transactions. 

With risk-based authentication, many merchants can process more valid purchases while saving additional verification steps for high-risk transactions. Alongside fast, automated decisioning, merchants can keep checkouts moving smoothly and more quickly – without exposing themselves to fraud.

title: Onramper Launches Chrome Extension for Crypto Quote Comparison
snippet: The Amsterdam fiat-to-crypto aggregator is bringing live quotes from 30+ licensed providers into Chrome's side panel for in-browser buying. The post Onramper Launches Chrome Extension for Crypto Quote Comparison appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Onramper, the Amsterdam-based fiat-to-crypto onramp aggregator, has launched a Chrome browser extension that lets users compare live crypto purchase quotes from more than thirty licensed providers without navigating away from their current page. The extension is available now on the Chrome Web Store.

The product surfaces in Chrome’s side panel, pulling quotes from Onramper’s existing provider network and displaying them alongside one another in the user’s local currency. Users can buy, sell or swap, select their preferred provider and complete a transaction without opening a new tab. Onramper and the chosen provider handle identity verification and payment processing at checkout. The extension supports more than 170 local payment methods, including card, bank transfer, Apple Pay and Google Pay, with availability varying by country.

How it works

Rick Thomas, co-CEO at Onramper

The extension is positioned as a comparison layer, not a standalone exchange. Users who connect a wallet can also swap tokens directly from the panel. Up to five wallet addresses can be saved under custom names, with a one-click copy function at checkout. Localised currency display and preset transaction amounts are applied automatically based on the user’s country.

Privacy features include no embedded analytics or tracking. Settings and saved wallet addresses are stored locally in the browser, with cross-device sync disabled by default and a single-action data-erasure option in the settings menu.

Onramper co-chief executive Rick Thomas framed the launch as a structural shift in how crypto access is delivered. “Crypto has treated the on-ramp as a destination: a separate site, a separate tab, a separate decision. As the industry matures, buying has to happen where people already are, and with more providers and payment methods in every market, comparing them should not be a research project,” he said.

Onramper’s existing client list includes Exodus, Coinbase, Jupiter, Kraken and pump.fun, providing the company with meaningful distribution through its widget and API business before this consumer-facing extension.

Market context

The fiat-to-crypto onramp segment has consolidated around a small number of aggregators over the past two years, with players such as MoonPay, Transak and Ramp Network competing alongside Onramper for integrations with wallets and Web3 applications. The browser-extension route is a distinct channel rather than a direct challenge to those B2B integrations: it targets end users directly and reduces friction at the point of discovery rather than at the point of application onboarding.

That consumer-facing angle carries regulatory considerations that the B2B widget business largely bypasses. Direct-to-user crypto purchasing tools must comply with the applicable financial promotion rules in each jurisdiction. In the UK, the Financial Conduct Authority‘s crypto financial promotions regime, which came into full effect in 2024, imposes strict approval requirements on the marketing of qualifying cryptoassets. The EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation introduces further conduct obligations for firms serving retail customers across member states. The extension’s routing model, in which Onramper aggregates and displays quotes but the selected licensed provider executes the transaction, may limit Onramper’s direct regulatory exposure in some markets, though that determination will depend on how individual regulators characterise the aggregation activity.

The near-term measure of success for the extension will be

adoption volume and whether the browser channel converts browsers into buyers at a meaningfully higher rate than tab-switching behaviour currently allows. Onramper has not disclosed a target user number or a timeline for expanding availability beyond Chrome.

title: Klarna launches AI ‘concierge’
snippet: The buy now, pay later provider has waded into agentic commerce with a new tool and aims to expand its longer-term loan portfolio.
fullText:
Dive Brief:

Klarna Group introduced a personal artificial intelligence assistant this week to complement its core consumer lending business, and is debuting it through waitlist invitations, the buy now, pay later company said Tuesday.

“We are bringing AI and agentic commerce to the core of Klarna,” CEO Sebastian Siemiatkowski said Tuesday on a quarterly earnings call with analysts. Klarna users have spent about $34 billion since 2020 using the web browser feature in the existing app, the company said in a press release.

Separately, Klarna said it’s aiming to expand its longer-term installment loans to more U.S. and European consumers. Those loans are Klarna’s fastest-growing and “highest-earning product per dollar of volume,” the company said in its earnings release.

Dive Insight:

Klarna’s AI tool acts as “a personal concierge” for tasks such as booking reservations, drafting email replies, shopping and sending upcoming birthday reminders, the company said in its press release.

The assistant will not complete purchases autonomously – a human is required to authorize payments, a Klarna spokesperson said. Transactions through the AI tool are through a Klarna payment method or a user’s debit card, the spokesperson said. 

The agent interacts via text message and is also available via Meta Platforms’ WhatsApp and Apple’s iMessage text services. The company spokesperson declined to say how many people have been invited to use the assistant so far.

The Klarna tool enters a crowded field of personal AI agents, with consumer offerings that include shopping abilities from Meta’s Muse, Google’s Gemini, Instinct, OpenAI’s dots and Daydream, a New York-based online search and shopping fashion startup. ByteDance, the Beijing-based parent of social media platform TikTok outside the U.S., also plans to release a personal AI agent, Bloomberg News reported last week.

As Klarna bots begin shopping, the company is keen to grow beyond its traditional zero-interest pay later loans. That retail-based lending still accounts for about three-quarters of the company’s gross merchandise volume.

Much of the growth for the lengthier “fair financing” loans has been in the U.S., where the company has partnered with merchants such as Airbnb, Walmart and Southwest Airlines.

Longer-term financing is available at 21% of Klarna’s affiliated merchants, or 283,000, up from about 150,000 a year ago, the company said.

Volume for these loans has more than doubled over the past 12 months, to $12.5 billion, compared to $6 billion in the rest of the world, Klarna said in its earnings report. The company also called out Europe as a region for growth. In the U.S., Klarna’s longer duration loans have terms up to three years and interest rates to a maximum of 35.99%.

For these loans, Klarna targets a transaction margin of 3% to 4% of volume, or “more than three times” what the traditional pay later loans earn, the company said in its earnings report.

For the third quarter, Klarna reported a net loss of $65 million, compared to a $95 million loss in the same period last year. Revenue rose 12% to $1 billion. Active users rose 7% from a year ago, to 122 million in 26 countries.

Klarna also projected a profit for the last three months of 2026, citing “a good start” to the quarter.

The earnings call was expected to be the last for Klarna CFO Niclas Neglen, who is leaving the company at year-end to become the chief financial officer at Adyen, the Amsterdam-based payments processor.

Last week, Klarna announced that Chris Koegel, a vice president at Robinhood Markets, the trading and personal finance platform, will become its new CFO effective Jan. 1.

title: N26 and Franklin Templeton to Launch Digital Retirement Account in Germany
snippet: N26 partners with Franklin Templeton to launch a digital, state-subsidised private retirement account in Germany on 1 January 2027. The post N26 and Franklin Templeton to Launch Digital Retirement Account in Germany appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
European digital bank N26 has announced a strategic partnership with global asset manager Franklin Templeton to launch a fully digital, state-subsidised private retirement account (Altersvorsorgedepot) in Germany. Scheduled to go live on 1 January 2027—subject to regulatory certification—the new product integrates long-term, capital market-based retirement investing directly alongside everyday banking within the N26 mobile app.

Mike Dargan, CEO at N26

The rollout comes ahead of Germany’s upcoming pension reform, which is designed to modernize how consumers build long-term financial security through exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and capital markets. Pre-registration for the retirement account is already open inside the N26 app for existing customers.

“At N26, we are making building a financial future feel as straightforward as managing money day to day,” stated Mike Dargan, chief executive officer at N26. “The pension reform in Germany is a transformational moment, allowing millions to change the way they plan for retirement. With Franklin Templeton as our partner, we are excited to deliver a modern digital solution that sits in your banking app, right by your investments, savings, and everyday finances, to help everyone take this important first step within the same N26 ecosystem they know and trust.”

Dual Portfolio Architecture and Fee Structure

Jenny Johnson, CEO at Franklin Templeton

Under the partnership, Franklin Templeton serves as N26’s exclusive investment and product partner for the default portfolio option, providing underlying investment infrastructure, proprietary ETF capabilities, and portfolio expertise. Users will be able to select between two distinct investment structures:

Standard Portfolio (Standarddepot): A pre-configured portfolio split between two fund categories. Customers who open a Standard portfolio by June 2027 receive a permanent N26 service fee exemption, while sign-ups from July 2027 onward incur a 0.10 per cent annual service fee. Furthermore, total expense ratios (TERs) are completely waived until the end of 2028 before reverting to 0.09 per cent.

Self-Directed Portfolio (Selbstentscheiderdepot): Allows investors to construct custom portfolios from a selection of more than 300 eligible funds managed by Franklin Templeton, Amundi, Deutsche Asset Management (Xtrackers), and Vanguard. Trades are priced at €0.90 per order, while automated savings plans remain free across both portfolio tiers and all eligible assets.

“Germany has a strong savings culture, and as its population ages, helping more people move from saving to investing for their future is increasingly important,” added Jenny Johnson, chief executive officer at Franklin Templeton. “By combining Franklin Templeton’s investment expertise with N26’s digital banking platform, we can make investing simpler and more accessible, helping more people put their savings to work and take greater ownership of their financial future.”

State Subsidies and Early-Adopter Incentives

Both the Standard and Self-directed portfolios qualify for German government retirement grants, requiring a minimum annual contribution of €120 to unlock state subsidies. Under the basic grant (Grundzulage), the state matches 50 per cent of the first €360 contributed and 25 per cent of subsequent deposits up to €1,800, providing up to €540 in annual government support—with additional bonuses available for parents and savers under the age of 25.

To accelerate early adoption ahead of and immediately following the January launch, N26 is offering promotional incentives valid until March 2027:

Initial Kickstart Bonus: Customers receive a 10 per cent bonus of up to €250 on their initial deposit, credited directly into their retirement account within 30 days.

Monthly Savings Match: N26 will match 10 per cent of monthly savings plan contributions up to €15 per month for the first 12 months following the initial deposit.

Headquartered in Berlin with a workforce of 1,600 employees across European hubs including Barcelona, Madrid, Milan, Paris, and Vienna, N26 operates under a full German banking license across 24 markets. By embedding state-certified retirement infrastructure into a mobile-first interface, N26 and Franklin Templeton aim to lower barriers to capital market participation as Germany overhauls its national pension framework.

title: Zowie Expands AI Customer-Service Agents into Romania
snippet: The Polish AI firm is opening a Bucharest office, backed by $20m in prior funding, targeting banks, telecoms and insurers in a low-adoption market. The post Zowie Expands AI Customer-Service Agents into Romania appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Zowie, a Warsaw-based AI platform serving enterprise customer service, is entering Romania as its first market in Central and Eastern Europe beyond Poland. The company plans to open an office in Bucharest and has begun hiring an account executive and a sales development representative for the Romanian market. The expansion will be funded from existing revenue and the company’s cumulative $20 million in prior funding, which was raised from investors including Tiger Global, Gradient Ventures (Google’s AI fund), Alt Capital and Inovo.

The move follows demand signals from large Romanian enterprises in the sectors Zowie already serves at home: banking, insurance, telecoms, logistics and retail. Named customers on the platform include InPost, Allianz and Decathlon, and the platform processes more than 100 million conversations a year.

 The gap Zowie is targeting

Maja Schaefer, co-founder and CEO of Zowie

Romania presents an unusually wide enterprise AI adoption gap. Eurostat figures for 2025 put the EU average share of enterprises using AI technologies at 20 per cent. Romania recorded the lowest share in the bloc at 5.2 per cent, compared with Poland at 8.4 per cent and Bulgaria at 8.5 per cent. Among large enterprises specifically, the contrast is starker: only 21 per cent of large Romanian companies use AI against an EU average of 55 per cent. Zowie’s chief executive, Maja Schaefer, framed that gap in operational rather than aspirational terms.

“Most large CEE banks, telecoms and retailers already have a chatbot. Very few of them resolve the customer’s problem, and there is a significant room for improvement in how the process is measured. That is the gap we work in,” said Schaefer, who co-founded the company with chief revenue officer Maciej Ciołek in 2019.

Zowie’s product architecture is built around the distinction between conversation and execution. The conversational layer runs on large language models, while actions taken on behalf of a customer, changing a tariff plan, verifying identity, opening a parcel locker, are handled by a deterministic engine that follows rules the enterprise sets. Escalation to a human agent is designed in, not bolted on. That combination is intended to satisfy the compliance requirements of regulated sectors such as banking and insurance, where the consequences of an incorrect automated action carry regulatory weight.

Market context and competitive positioning

The CEE enterprise AI customer-service market is at an early stage, but several large vendors and regional integrators are already present. Global platforms such as Salesforce Einstein, Genesys and LivePerson compete in the contact-centre automation space, while a growing number of European AI agent start-ups are targeting the same regulated-sector buyer profile. Zowie’s competitive argument rests on production depth rather than demo-stage capability: the InPost deployment, which handles customer calls across Poland, the United Kingdom and France and can open a parcel locker mid-call, offers a concrete reference case for logistics and retail buyers.

From a regulatory perspective, enterprises deploying AI agents in banking and insurance across the EU face a tightening framework. The EU AI Act classifies certain AI systems in credit and insurance as high-risk, requiring conformity assessments, human oversight provisions and transparency obligations. A vendor that can demonstrate a deterministic, rule-governed execution layer alongside the language model component is better placed to support clients through those requirements than one offering a purely generative interface.

Romania is also the region’s second-largest economy after Poland, and adoption of language technologies among its large enterprises roughly doubled year on year according to the same Eurostat dataset, suggesting the laggard position may be closing faster than headline figures indicate.

title: Why “faster cash flow” sells embedded payments to US SMBs
snippet: New research shows 65% of US SMBs use embedded payments, and what it takes to win the rest.
fullText:
Why “faster cash flow” sells embedded payments to US SMBs

A new Adyen and Visa report surveyed 500 US SMBs on why they adopt embedded payments and what they need next.

65% of US SMBs take payments inside the software they already use to run their business. Of the third that don't, nearly one in three say they're considering it within the next year.

For SaaS platforms, the opportunity is twofold: win new adoption and deepen existing relationships. 

Both come down to the same thing: knowing what SMBs want payments to do for them.

To find out, Adyen and Visa surveyed 500 US SMBs between January and March 2026. Here are four key learnings: 

1. SMBs want faster cash flow

55% of US SMBs said they adopted embedded payments to get paid faster. 

It reflects the operating environment facing many SMBs today. Rising costs, tighter margins and financial uncertainty mean faster payouts can have a direct impact on business performance.

For SaaS platforms, this is where to start the conversation. Leading with “faster cash flow” will resonate more strongly than technical features alone.  

2. SMBs understand the time saved, not the revenue gained 

For SMBs who already use embedded payments, they focus primarily on operational wins. Or, what they’re more likely to notice in their day-to-day:

88% say they get paid faster and more reliably

88% say checkouts improved for their customers

86% say they spend less time on admin

Ask about growth, however and it goes quieter. Few connect embedded payments to more revenue. 

It suggests that adoption is often driven by solving an immediate challenge — billing, reconciliation and reporting — rather than a clear awareness of embedded payments as a category.

That nuance matters. For SaaS platforms, the fix is to show that saving time is only half the story. A better checkout experience, for example, means fewer lost sales and more completed transactions.

3. 

SMBs who haven't switched think what they've got is fine

For the SMBs, who aren’t considering embedded payments, 51% say their current payment setup “works well”. 

Traditional or legacy setups were chosen years ago, and as far as they’re concerned, they’re fine. 

To win with these SMBs, software platforms need to build a compelling case for making the switch: better cash flow, less manual work and a more connected checkout experience. 

Of those who are considering embedding payments, their hesitations are more specific:

30% want to keep payments separate, for control or simplicity

26% assume it will cost them more

25% aren't confident the payment methods they need are covered

Platforms can answer each of these with proof points: how much admin time is saved with an integrated setup, what those hours are worth against the fees and the range of payment methods that are covered.

4. When SMBs need a loan, they don't ask their software platform

Banks remain the main source of borrowing for US SMBs. 

According to the survey, 42% borrow from a bank, while 16% borrow from the platform they already run their business on. 

Yet the qualities SMBs value most — a simple application, competitive rates and fast approval — are areas where platform-based financing can offer a compelling alternative.

But trust remains critical. 

Financial products require a deeper relationship than payments alone, so platforms need to establish value through the everyday experiences SMBs rely on, like getting paid on time, before extending into broader financial services.

Adoption is growing, but earning trust is key 

The US market is past the point of persuasion. 

SMBs aren't waiting to be convinced that embedded payments work. They're deciding which platform is worth trusting with more of their business.

title: Act now to be resilient in the quantum future
snippet: Quantum computing will bring significant opportunities to the UK financial sector, but firms need to act now to prepare for a world where a viable hostile quantum computer could break today’s widely used cryptography standards.The financial sector depends on secure information and communication. Cryptography – of which encryption is just one part – helps firms protect their clients’ data, verify who they are dealing with, and maintain trust in their systems.Sufficiently powerful quantum computers pose a real threat to that security. Quantum computing will bring significant opportunities to the UK financial sector, but firms need to act now to prepare for a world where a viable hostile quantum computer could break today’s widely used cryptography standards.

The financial sector depends on secure information and communication. Cryptography – of which encryption is just one part – helps firms protect their clients’ data, verify who they are dealing with, and maintain trust in their systems.

Sufficiently powerful quantum computers pose a real threat to that security. Without trustworthy cryptography, consumers would face fraud, firms would suffer operational disruption, and the integrity of financial transactions and markets would be put at risk.

That’s why we are talking to firms about preparing for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) now. We don’t know for certain when a viable quantum computer will emerge, but the coming years will likely see the technology advance at a rapid pace.

Preparing for this new world requires firms to understand where and how they use cryptography and to be able to migrate all hardware and software to PQC, while managing operational risks.

Realistically, for most firms, this will require significant time, investment and effort.

What firms need to do now

So, what kind of timescale are we talking about? The National Centre for Cyber Security (NCSC) recommends 3 key milestones:

By 2028, firms complete a PQC migration plan.

By 2031, firms carry out high-priority migration activities.

By 2035, firms have migrated all systems, services and products to PQC.

Firms should not wait for these milestones before acting and where it is safe to do so, they should seek to be ready sooner. In line with NCSC guidance, we expect firms to act now to: 

Have a thorough and accurate understanding of the cryptography in place across systems and information.

Set clear, achievable, safe and risk-based migration objectives..

Implement migration plans and monitor, test and validate the changes, adjusting them where necessary.

Senior managers should ensure that their firms allocate enough time, investment and resources to manage PQC migration safely and meet the relevant deadlines. Failed change projects accounted for around a fifth of all incidents reported to us in 2025.

How we are supporting firms

We are trialling a new supervisory self-assessment tool with an initial sample of firms and intend to extend it to other firms in due course. This will help firms assess the maturity of their plans and help us understand the industry’s preparedness for PQC migration.

This trial will also help us identify common challenges and examples of good practice, which we intend to share with the sector.

We shared relevant insights from firms in April 2026 and will continue to engage with the industry through our Cyber Coordination Groups (CCGs), the Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG), and trade bodies and associations.

We will also consult on cyber resilience guidance for firms, including our expectations for how firms should address PQC risks through their cryptographic controls.

title: In Profile: Howard Wu, CEO, Provable
snippet: Howard Wu, co-founder and CEO of Provable, discusses blockchain privacy, confidential stablecoins, AI agents and the future of digital finance. The post In Profile: Howard Wu, CEO, Provable appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
There’s plenty of enthusiasm for moving money and financial assets onto blockchains. But how comfortable would businesses and consumers be if everyone could see what they were doing with that money?

As stablecoins and tokenised assets find more uses in financial services, privacy and security are becoming bigger priorities alongside speed and efficiency.

In this week’s In Profile, The Fintech Times catches up with Howard Wu, co-founder and CEO of Provable, a blockchain privacy technology company, to discuss his early days in crypto, the push to make digital finance more private and his predictions for the future of the industry.

Tell us more about your company and its purpose

We’re focused on confidential finance. I think there’s a pretty basic problem with the way money works in crypto today. If I use cash or pay with a credit card, that transaction isn’t available for everyone on the internet to see. But if I pay using Bitcoin or Ethereum, the transaction is public. I’ve always thought that’s a broken way for money to work. I wouldn’t want my mother using a system like that.

At Provable, we’re building the technology to do something about it. We developed Aleo, a blockchain that uses zero-knowledge cryptography so applications can verify transactions without making all the underlying information public. We’re also building products that make this technology accessible to developers and users.

Ultimately, we want people to be able to bring their banking and financial activities onchain without worrying about exposing that information to everybody else. That doesn’t mean giving up accountability. Financial systems still need to be secure and auditable, with information available to those who need to see it.

For us, confidentiality is the missing piece, and we’re focused on building products that people will actually want to use.

What are some of your recent achievements you’d like to highlight?

In February, we launched Shield Wallet, which lets people store and move assets privately on Aleo. That includes stablecoins such as USDCx, backed one-to-one by USDC held through Circle’s xReserve infrastructure.

Then, in August, we opened early access to Shield Swap, our confidential trading venue. When we were developing it, we met with a trading firm that believed its activity couldn’t be traced because it used different wallet addresses across several blockchains. We tested that assumption and, within a few hours, managed to link several addresses and reconstruct a large part of its trading activity for the quarter.

That tells you something about the problem we’re trying to solve. Professional traders don’t want competitors seeing their positions and strategies. Shield Swap lets them keep that information confidential while making market data, including prices and trade sizes, publicly verifiable.

We’ve also made progress in bringing this technology to more users. USDCx is now accessible through Kraken and supported in Ledger Wallet, and we’ve announced a collaboration with Flowdesk to bring institutional liquidity to Shield Swap.

More recently, we released Shield Wallet MCP, which allows AI agents to interact with the wallet. We’ve been very deliberate about giving users control over what those agents are allowed to do, whether that’s reading a balance or executing a trade. As AI starts handling more financial activity, I think those controls are going to be incredibly important.

How did you get into the industry?

I got into crypto when I was still in high school. I’ve always been interested in computers, and I used to spend a lot of time reading technology blogs. One day I came across an article about this new form of internet money called Bitcoin, and I was fascinated by it.

By the time I got to UC Berkeley, all sorts of other cryptocurrencies were appearing. I started researching how blockchain networks reached agreement on transactions, which eventually led me to learn about cryptography.

Around then, a professor called Alessandro Chiesa had just arrived at Berkeley from MIT. I was an undergraduate who really wanted to get involved in cryptography research, so I cold-emailed him. We ended up working together on libsnark, a cryptographic library that went on to be used in Zcash.

From there, we started exploring whether we could build a blockchain that supported private smart contracts. That work led to Zexe, and in 2019 we founded Aleo to commercialise the idea.

What’s the best thing about working in this industry?

When I started out, we were working on mathematical problems that hardly anyone outside cryptography was thinking about. Now people are using that research to build financial products. I still find that pretty remarkable.

I also think we’re still very early. There’s so much financial activity that hasn’t moved onchain yet, and I find the prospect of helping build the systems that make that possible really motivating.

What frustrates you most about the fintech industry?

What frustrates me is how often privacy and compliance are treated as though they’re incompatible, particularly in crypto. I think we’ve got that completely wrong.

Privacy is one of those things people only appreciate when it’s too late. Look at age verification online. People are being asked to upload passports and driving licences just to prove they’re over 18. We’re creating enormous databases of sensitive personal information that become targets for hackers.

We’ve built zPass, for example, so someone can prove they’re over 18 without handing over their date of birth or home address. Why should an age check require everything else on your driving license? We can use the same technology in finance, keeping personal information private while giving regulators access to what they need.

The technology exists. I just wish more regulators and policymakers understood what’s already possible.

How have your previous roles influenced your career?

Most of my career has been spent on the research and engineering side of crypto, so I haven’t followed the traditional route through financial services.

I learned pretty much everything I knew about cryptography from my advisor Alessandro. He was incredibly meticulous, very process-oriented, and he had a real discipline about his work. I don’t think I’d have developed that same approach without him.

In the early days, we were writing zero-knowledge circuits by hand. You could make a tiny mistake in the code and spend hours trying to figure out what had gone wrong. It was incredibly frustrating, and that experience influenced our decision to develop Leo, a programming language that makes it easier for developers to build private applications.

I’ve carried a lot of those lessons into Provable. The research is fascinating, but you also have to think about how people are actually going to use what you’re building.

What’s the best mistake you’ve ever made?

Probably not enjoying university enough! I honestly wish I could go back and live it up a little more.

Then again, I was 22 when Zcash launched in 2016. We’d spent years on the research behind it, and suddenly there was a financial system running on software I’d helped develop. That’s quite something to experience at that age. So I’m not sure I’d change much.

So perhaps I missed out on a bit of student life, but I can’t complain too much about where it took me.

What has the future got in store for your company?

There’s a big opportunity with financial institutions. As more assets move onchain, banks and investment businesses are going to need ways to protect their customers’ information, portfolios and trading activity. We want to make that possible without sacrificing the security and accountability that blockchain technology offers.

We’re also building on our work with AI agents, looking at how they can interact safely with financial systems and making sure people can control what those agents access and do on their behalf.

What are the next key talking points or challenges for your industry as a whole?

Stablecoins have dominated the conversation over the past year, but now people are starting to talk about private stablecoins. I think that’s going to be a major focus as more financial institutions move onchain. They’re not going to want their clients’ portfolios and transaction histories available for everyone to see.

AI agents are another big area to watch. We’re moving towards a world where software can make payments and execute trades on our behalf, but those systems can be manipulated. You can’t eliminate the risk of prompt injection entirely, so giving people proper control over what their agents can access and do is incredibly important.

Then there’s quantum computing. Today’s blockchain protocols need to prepare for a future where quantum computers could compromise existing cryptography. We have promising approaches to post-quantum security, but they come with challenges around storage and scalability that the industry still needs to solve.

We’re still looking at what I’d call toy examples of financial markets today. The amount of money onchain is tiny compared with the wider financial system. But I think that once serious money starts moving onto blockchains, confidentiality will become a basic requirement. My prediction is that more than 90 per cent of stablecoin payments will be private by 2030.

title: OpenAI wallet taps card networks
snippet: The artificial intelligence company has created a digital wallet through which its ChatGPT agent can use Visa, Mastercard and American Express.
fullText:
Artificial intelligence company OpenAI last week launched its inaugural digital wallet for use by its ChatGPT agent, enabling it to make purchases by way of the major card networks.

It’s one of the first instances in the evolving agentic commerce world of an AI agent using Visa, Mastercard or American Express to automatically pay for a transaction based on initial instructions to the AI agent. Mastercard also announced a first-time airfare purchase last week.

The card networks have been working with AI companies to set protocols for agentic commerce, but they’ve all tempered expectations by saying the new bot-driven commerce is in its early stages of development. AI companies and payments providers are racing to set standards for such transactions to help consumers feel comfortable that there will be safeguards when AI agents get their orders wrong, or in cases of fraud.

“We’re introducing ChatGPT Wallet, setting a new bar for secure payments by agents,” OpenAI said in a Friday post. “It’s the first wallet that lets agents pay without access to users’ actual card details and that requires a security check for every purchase, while also preserving existing card rewards and protections for eligible disputes.”

The card networks have also been working with other tech giants to create the agentic technology protocols, but also to set parameters for which companies shoulder responsibility and liability when transactions go awry. 

Google, with its Gemini agent, and Anthropic, with its Claude agent, are also competing in the agentic realm. In addition, digital payments player Stripe has connected its Link digital wallet to Meta’s Muse agent. 

The inaugural ChatGPT wallet transaction was completed using tokenized credentials so the agent is unable to see a cardholders’ card information, such as the security code and expiration date. 

Initially, the wallet feature will only be available to certain ChatGPT users, the OpenAI post said. It will also allow for card rewards and “eligible disputes.” 

Card company executives have suggested AI agents will not be widely used this year, but they have expressed enthusiasm for adding the new channel of commerce.

“Innovation starts slowly until it's sudden,” Visa’s president of value-added services, Andrew Torre, said last week at the KBW Fintech Ecosystem Conference. “What you've seen over the course of the last month, or two months is real interest in agentic commerce.”

“Clients all over the world see this coming and want to get in our agentic sandbox,” Torre said Tuesday at the conference. “There is a lot of consumer interest and, of course, our clients want to be there where their consumers want to be.”

The ChatGPT wallet transaction is the first Amex agentic commerce integration, enabling card holders to engage in agent-facilitated purchases, a spokesperson for that company said by email.

“We're continuing to work with leading AI and commerce partners on additional integrations to bring trusted agentic payments and Amex Membership value into the experiences Card Members are increasingly using,” the Amex spokesperson said.

While ChatGPT’s wallet capabilities are landing just as the U.S. year-end holiday shopping season gets started, executives and analysts don’t expect the new commerce to spool up until next year, at the earliest. 

That’s partly because some significant players involved in digital commerce, including banks and major retailers, are still not ready to participate in AI-based payments. For instance, Amazon and United Airlines have blocked some agentic activity on their websites.

“We should see a lot more agentic commerce happening in 2027 as personal agents become more popular and get more adoption,” Boston Consulting Group Managing Director Inderpreet Batra said in an interview last month.

OpenAI acknowledged in its post that its “early days” for agentic commerce, noting that transactions won’t work if websites block agents or if payment systems don’t recognize agents. 

“We’re starting with limited availability to ChatGPT Pro users, so we can learn from real-world use and work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to improve compatibility and reliability,” the OpenAI post said.

title: SFF 2026 Opens This Week to Address Rewiring of Global Finance
snippet: Singapore FinTech Festival 2026 kicks off this week at Singapore EXPO, uniting global leaders to examine how technology, geoeconomics, capital, talent, and policy are rewiring finance. The post SFF 2026 Opens This Week to Address Rewiring of Global Finance appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The 11th edition of the Singapore FinTech Festival (SFF) 2026 kicks off this week at the Singapore EXPO, running from 18 to 20 November to convene global leaders across policy, finance, and technology. Organised by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Global Finance & Technology Network (GFTN) in collaboration with The Association of Banks in Singapore (ABS), the flagship event builds on SFF 2025, which drew more than 70,000 attendees from 142 countries and approximately 1,000 speakers.

Operating under the theme “The Coming Rewiring of the Financial System: New Risks. New Rules. New Growth”, SFF 2026 examines how five interconnected structural forces—technology, geoeconomics, capital, talent, and policy—are reshaping the global financial architecture.

Five Core Forces and Multi-Hall Exhibition

Through keynote addresses, policy dialogues, industry discussions, and technology demonstrations, the festival programme explores five primary pillars:

Technology: Examining how agentic artificial intelligence, tokenisation, digital money, and quantum technologies are transforming financial services and transactions.

Geoeconomics: Assessing how shifts in global trade, capital flows, and international cooperation are altering the financial landscape.

Capital: Exploring strategies for mobilising capital to support innovation, infrastructure, and economic growth.

Talent: Addressing the implications of artificial intelligence for jobs, workforce skills, and entrepreneurship.

Policy: Evaluating how regulatory frameworks are evolving to support financial innovation while safeguarding trust, resilience, and financial stability.

Across five exhibition halls, SFF 2026 hosts over 600 sponsors and exhibitors alongside more than 40 international pavilions. The exhibition showcases advancements in agentic commerce, AI-enabled payments, digital assets, cross-border settlement, and programmable financial infrastructure, while offering dedicated platforms for startups to connect with investors and workforce capacity-building programmes.

“The decisions we make today about technology, regulation and financial infrastructure will shape how finance serves businesses and individuals for years to come,” stated Kenneth Gay, chief finTech officer at MAS. “As AI, digital money and other innovations transform the financial system, we need to make sure that innovation goes hand in hand with trust and resilience. SFF 2026 brings together leaders from across finance, technology and policy to exchange ideas, tackle common challenges and shape the next chapter of global finance.”

“Global finance is undergoing a structural transformation driven by five interconnected forces: technology, geoeconomics, capital, talent and policy,” added Sopnendu Mohanty, group chief executive officer at GFTN. “Together, they are reshaping financial markets, redirecting capital flows, and redefining both jobs and the institutions that underpin economic growth. SFF’s critical role is to bring together global leaders in Singapore to translate these shifts into coherent policy, trusted financial infrastructure and new opportunities for employment and growth across borders.”

SME Financing, Cross-Border Pavilions, and Founder Programmes

This year’s festival introduces new initiatives focused on small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) financing and international market connectivity:

12th Global SME Finance Forum: Held in conjunction with SFF under the theme “Transforming Access to Impact: Market, Capital & Technology”, the event is organised by the World Bank Group-managed SME Finance Forum in partnership with GFTN. Convening C-level leaders from more than 80 countries, the forum features the annual Global SME Finance Awards, an innovation Experience Centre, and a dedicated Learning Day.

India Pavilion: Presented by the Indian Trade Promotion Organisation under India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry, the pavilion connects Indian startups, financial institutions, regulators, and policymakers with Singapore’s capital markets to deepen bilateral economic ties and facilitate ASEAN and global market access.

GFTN & SEGA Go-Global Pavilion: Featuring 30 technology companies from Shanghai and Shenzhen, this initiative builds on GFTN’s partnership with Shanghai’s Huangpu District to connect Chinese innovators with international investors and financial institutions.

Alongside these additions, SFF 2026 brings back its signature programmes—including SFF MeetUp, expected to facilitate more than 20,000 pre-scheduled meetings; Investor Hours, connecting founders with general and limited partners; and The Founders Peak™, featuring TED-inspired sessions with global entrepreneurs. The festival also features the launch of STUBBORN: Decoding the Unreasonable Mindset of Founders Who Build Against All Odds, a book drawing on four years of fieldwork analyzing 350 founder journeys across more than 40 countries.

Insights2040 Annual Meetings Set the Stage

Preceding the main festival from 16 to 17 November, the invitation-only Insights2040 Annual Meetings convene senior public- and private-sector leaders in an expanded dedicated space on Level 5 of the Sands Expo & Convention Centre. Conducted under the Chatham House Rule, the closed-door dialogues examine establishing accountability and liability in agentic systems, addressing challenges in scaling tokenised markets, developing global frameworks and shared best practices in payment chains, and taking stock of sovereignty and resilience in a rewired financial system.

The Federal Reserve is also instituting a new access fee that it says will create a more “streamlined experience” for its bank clients.

        

            

        Published Nov. 17, 2026
